aathira varier & subrata panda Mumbai, 18 November The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has asked banks, small ﬁnance banks (SFBs), and non-banking ﬁnancial companies (NBFCs) to strengthen controls around appli- cation programming interfaces (APIs), tighten safeguards for third-party systems, and improve monitoring of fund transfers amid a rise in cyberattacks targeting ﬁnancial institutions, according to senior bankers Business Standard spoke to. The RBI issued an advisory on November 16 focusing on API security and governance, particu- larly API-based fund transfers. The regulator has also been com- municating its expectations to lenders through regular advisories and discussions, extending its engagement to NBFCs. “There have been discussions, and banks have been advised to remain cautious. These advisories and discussions are happening regularly, almost on a weekly basis. The RBI has been communi- cating what banks should be doing and what it expects regulated entities to implement. The regula- tor is also reaching out to NBFCs,” said a senior banker at a private- sector bank. A key concern is the exploitation of vulnerabilities in third-party systems connected to banks and NBFCs. In some instances, fraudsters have com- promised the systems of ﬁnancial entities to divert money through banking channels. In other cases, beneﬁciary account details in loan disbursement systems have been manipulated, resulting in funds being transferred to accounts con- trolled by fraudsters. These are essentially supply- chain attacks, in which a weakness in one participant’s systems can expose other entities connected to it. Banks are therefore being asked to strengthen API controls rather than rely entirely on the security arrangements of their partners.“The basic idea is that institutions should not assume everything is secure at the other end simply because they are receiving transaction requests through an API. They need to introduce additional controls and checks to establish whether a transaction is legitimate and whether the instructions have been properly authorised by the partner,” said a senior banker fam- iliar with the RBI’s advisories. The safeguards being empha- sised include transaction velocity checks, rate limits on API requests, whitelisting and encryption, pre- validation of beneﬁciary accounts, and more frequent reconciliation of transactions. Lenders also need to periodically rotate API auth- entication keys and introduce additional checks when transac- tions appear abnormal. Banks have been asked to review the security arrangements of their counterparties as well. The RBI’s advisories have covered different aspects of the problem, including loan disburse- ments and direct APIs used for fund transfers. Banks had initially been asked to re-examine existing controls, including limits on the number of fund transfer requests that can be initiated through APIs within a speciﬁed period, regular monitoring of transaction vol- umes, and the use of throttling mechanisms wherever necessary. Beyond API security, the regu- lator is also focusing on third- party risk management, data protection and incident response. Lenders are expected to proac- tively assess their exposure to cyber risks rather than limit their response to reporting incidents after they occur. “The focus is on the prepared- ness of institutions, particularly banks, to ensure that they are not merely responding to a cyber inci- dent after it occurs. They should proactively assess their own expo- sure, protect the interests of cus- tomers and other stakeholders, and maintain the resilience of the banking ecosystem,” said another senior banker. Regulated entities are currently required to report certain cyber incidents to the RBI within six hours. However, lenders are also expected to strengthen internal response mechanisms, including senior-level monitoring, root cause analysis, corrective action, and forensic investigations, wherever necessary. They need to have mechanisms in place to restore sys- tems and recover operational capa- bilities following an attack.
